title: Characters Form an Orthonormal Basis
---

We know that $\chi_1, \ldots, \chi_k$ are orthonormal in $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$, so they are linearly independent and $k$ is at most the number of conjugacy classes. We now prove that they also span $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$, so that $k$ equals the number of conjugacy classes. The proof uses a weighted version of the averaging projection.

## <span class="num">13.6.1</span> Weighted Averages

:::proposition{13.6.1} Weighted averaging operators
Let $\alpha$ be a class function on $G$ and $V$ a representation of $G$, and let $$\varphi_{\alpha, V} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\alpha(g)\,g : V \to V.$$ Then $\varphi_{\alpha, V}$ is a homomorphism of representations, and $\Tr\varphi_{\alpha, V} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\alpha(g)\,\chi_V(g)$.
:::

:::proof
For $h \in G$, $$\begin{aligned}
h\,\varphi_{\alpha, V}\,h^{-1} &= \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\alpha(g)\,hgh^{-1} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g' \in G}\alpha(h^{-1}g'h)\,g' \\
&= \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g' \in G}\alpha(g')\,g' = \varphi_{\alpha, V},
\end{aligned}$$ where we substituted $g' = hgh^{-1}$, which runs over $G$ as $g$ does, and used that $\alpha$ is a class function. So $h\,\varphi_{\alpha, V} = \varphi_{\alpha, V}\,h$ for every $h \in G$. The trace formula follows from linearity of the trace.
:::

For the constant function $\alpha = 1$, $\varphi_{1, V}$ is the averaging projection $\varphi_V$ of Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1). We also note two simple facts. If $V = X \oplus Y$ is a direct sum of subrepresentations, then $\varphi_{\alpha, V}$ preserves $X$ and $Y$ and restricts to $\varphi_{\alpha, X}$ and $\varphi_{\alpha, Y}$ on them, because each $g$ does. If $\psi : X \to Y$ is an isomorphism of representations, then $\varphi_{\alpha, Y} = \psi\,\varphi_{\alpha, X}\,\psi^{-1}$, because $\rho_Y(g) = \psi\,\rho_X(g)\,\psi^{-1}$ for each $g$.

:::theorem{13.6.2} Irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis
The characters $\chi_1, \ldots, \chi_k$ of the irreducible representations of $G$ form an orthonormal basis of $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ with respect to $H$. Every class function $\beta$ on $G$ can be written as $$\beta = \sum_{i=1}^k H(\chi_i, \beta)\,\chi_i.$$ In particular, the number of irreducible representations of $G$, up to isomorphism, equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.
:::

:::proof
Orthonormality is Theorem [13.5.4](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#theorem-13-5-4). We first show that a class function $\alpha$ with $H(\alpha, \chi_i) = 0$ for all $i$ is zero.

The complex conjugate $\ol\alpha$ is also a class function. By Proposition [13.6.1](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#proposition-13-6-1), $\varphi_{\ol\alpha, V_i}$ is a homomorphism of representations $V_i \to V_i$, so by Schur’s Lemma it equals $c\,\id_{V_i}$ for some $c \in \CC$. Taking traces, $$n_ic = \Tr\varphi_{\ol\alpha, V_i} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\ol{\alpha(g)}\,\chi_i(g) = H(\alpha, \chi_i) = 0,$$ so $\varphi_{\ol\alpha, V_i} = 0$ for every $i$. Every representation $V$ is a direct sum of subrepresentations, each isomorphic to some $V_i$ (Corollary [13.2.3](/notes/math-55a/13-2-maschkes-theorem-and-complete-reducibility#corollary-13-2-3)), so by the two facts above, $\varphi_{\ol\alpha, V} = 0$ for every representation $V$. Take $V$ to be the regular representation $R$, and apply $\varphi_{\ol\alpha, R}$ to the basis vector $e_e$ indexed by the identity element: $$0 = \varphi_{\ol\alpha, R}(e_e) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\ol{\alpha(g)}\,e_g.$$ Since the $e_g$ are linearly independent, $\alpha(g) = 0$ for every $g \in G$.

Now let $\beta$ be any class function, and let $\alpha = \beta - \sum_i H(\chi_i, \beta)\,\chi_i$. For each $j$, orthonormality gives $H(\chi_j, \alpha) = H(\chi_j, \beta) - H(\chi_j, \beta) = 0$, hence $H(\alpha, \chi_j) = \ol{H(\chi_j, \alpha)} = 0$. By what we have shown, $\alpha = 0$, which is the stated formula for $\beta$. So $\chi_1, \ldots, \chi_k$ span $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ and form an orthonormal basis of it, and $k = \dim\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ is the number of conjugacy classes.
:::

:::corollary{13.6.3} Square character tables
The character table of a finite group is a square matrix.
:::

:::note
By Theorem [3.4.6](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-6), two permutations in $S_n$ are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type, and cycle types correspond to partitions of $n$. So the number of irreducible representations of $S_n$ is $p(n)$, the number of partitions of $n$. For instance $p(3) = 3$, in agreement with Proposition [13.3.5](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#proposition-13-3-5), while $p(4) = 5$ and $p(5) = 7$.
:::

## <span class="num">13.6.2</span> Projection onto Isotypic Components

Let $W$ be a representation with a decomposition $W = \bigoplus_j X_j$ into irreducible subrepresentations. The ***isotypic component*** of $W$ of type $V_i$ is the sum of those $X_j$ that are isomorphic to $V_i$; it is isomorphic to $V_i^{\oplus a_i}$, where $a_i$ is the multiplicity of $V_i$ in $W$. Weighted averages give an explicit projection onto it.

For irreducible $V_i$ and $V_j$, take $\alpha = \ol{\chi_i}$ in Proposition [13.6.1](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#proposition-13-6-1). As in the proof of Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2), $\varphi_{\ol{\chi_i}, V_j}$ is a scalar $c$ with $n_jc = H(\chi_i, \chi_j)$, so $$\varphi_{\ol{\chi_i}, V_j} = \frac{1}{n_j}H(\chi_i, \chi_j)\,\id_{V_j} = \begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{n_i}\,\id_{V_i} & \text{if } i = j, \\[1ex] 0 & \text{if } i \neq j. \end{cases}$$

:::proposition{13.6.4} Projection onto an isotypic component
Let $W$ be a representation of $G$, and let $$\pi_i = \frac{n_i}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\ol{\chi_i(g)}\,g : W \to W.$$ Then $\pi_i$ is the identity on every subrepresentation of $W$ isomorphic to $V_i$, and zero on every irreducible subrepresentation not isomorphic to $V_i$. Hence, for any decomposition of $W$ into irreducible subrepresentations, $\pi_i$ is the projection onto the isotypic component of type $V_i$ along the sum of the other isotypic components. In particular, this isotypic component is $\Img\pi_i$, so it does not depend on the decomposition.
:::

:::proof
We have $\pi_i = n_i\,\varphi_{\ol{\chi_i}, W}$. On an irreducible subrepresentation $X \cong V_j$, $\pi_i$ acts as $n_i\,\varphi_{\ol{\chi_i}, X}$, which is conjugate to $n_i\,\varphi_{\ol{\chi_i}, V_j}$. By the computation above, this is the identity if $j = i$ and zero otherwise.
:::

:::note
When $V_i$ is the trivial representation, $n_i = 1$ and $\chi_i = 1$, and $\pi_i$ is the averaging projection $\varphi_W$ onto $W^G$ of Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1).
:::

## <span class="num">13.6.3</span> Column Orthogonality

Orthonormality of the irreducible characters says that the rows of the character table are orthonormal, once the columns are weighted by the sizes of the classes. Because the table is square, its columns are orthogonal as well.

:::proposition{13.6.5} Column orthogonality
Let $C_1, \ldots, C_k$ be the conjugacy classes of $G$, with representatives $g_1, \ldots, g_k$. Then $$\sum_{i=1}^k\chi_i(g_s)\,\ol{\chi_i(g_t)} = \begin{cases}\dfrac{|G|}{|C_s|} & \text{if } s = t, \\[1ex] 0 & \text{if } s \neq t. \end{cases}$$
:::

:::proof
Let $X$ be the $k \times k$ matrix with entries $X_{is} = \chi_i(g_s)$, which is square by Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2), and let $D = \diag(|C_1|/|G|, \ldots, |C_k|/|G|)$. Orthonormality of the characters, written class by class, says $$\sum_{s=1}^k\ol{X_{is}}\,\frac{|C_s|}{|G|}\,X_{js} = \delta_{ij}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \ol{X}\,D\,X^t = I.$$ So the square matrix $\ol{X}D$ has inverse $X^t$, and therefore also $X^t\,\ol{X}D = I$, that is, $X^t\,\ol{X} = D^{-1}$. The $(s, t)$ entry of this identity is $\sum_i X_{is}\,\ol{X_{it}} = \delta_{st}\,|G|/|C_s|$.
:::

:::note
By Proposition [3.2.13](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-13), $|C_s| = [G : Z(g_s)]$, so $|G|/|C_s|$ is the order of the centralizer $Z(g_s) = \{h \in G : hg_s = g_sh\}$. Column orthogonality gives an independent check on a computed character table. It also shows that characters separate conjugacy classes: if $\chi_i(g) = \chi_i(h)$ for every $i$, then $\sum_i\chi_i(g)\,\ol{\chi_i(h)} = \sum_i|\chi_i(g)|^2 > 0$, so $g$ and $h$ lie in the same conjugacy class.
:::

:::exercise{13.6.6} Representations and Characters
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Decompose the permutation representation $\CC^3$ of $S_3$ into irreducibles using the inner product $H$.
2. Let $V$ be the standard representation of $S_3$. Use characters and the inner product $H$ to decompose $V \otimes V$, $\Sym^2 V$ and $\bigwedge^2 V$ into irreducibles, and compare with Example [13.3.6](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#example-13-3-6).
3. Compute the character table of the Klein four-group $\ZZ/2 \times \ZZ/2$. How many irreducible representations does it have, and what are their dimensions?
4. Let $G$ act on a finite set $S$, and let ${\CC}[S]$ be the permutation representation.

   <!-- list:paren-alpha -->

   1. Show that $\dim{\CC}[S]^G$ is the number of orbits of $G$ on $S$, and deduce Burnside’s lemma (Theorem [11.1.3](/notes/math-55a/11-1-orbits-stabilizers-and-burnsides-lemma#theorem-11-1-3)) from Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1).
   2. Suppose that $|S| \geq 2$ and that $G$ acts *doubly transitively*: for any two pairs $(s, t)$ and $(s', t')$ of distinct elements of $S$, there is $g \in G$ with $gs = s'$ and $gt = t'$. Show that ${\CC}[S] \cong \CC \oplus V_S$, where $\CC$ is the trivial representation and $V_S = \{\sum_s c_se_s : \sum_s c_s = 0\}$ is irreducible. Conclude that the standard representation of $S_n$ is irreducible for every $n \geq 2$.

:::solution
**(1)** The permutation character counts fixed points: $\chi(e) = 3$, $\chi((12)) = 1$, $\chi((123)) = 0$. With the class sizes $1, 3, 2$, $$H(\chi_U, \chi) = \tfrac16(3 + 3 + 0) = 1, \qquad H(\chi_{U'}, \chi) = \tfrac16(3 - 3 + 0) = 0,$$ and $H(\chi_V, \chi) = \frac16(6 + 0 + 0) = 1$. So $\CC^3 \cong U \oplus V$.

**(2)** The character of $V \otimes V$ is $\chi_V^2 = (4, 0, 1)$, and $$H(\chi_U, \chi_V^2) = \tfrac16(4 + 0 + 2) = 1, \qquad H(\chi_{U'}, \chi_V^2) = \tfrac16(4 + 0 + 2) = 1,$$ and $H(\chi_V, \chi_V^2) = \frac16(8 + 0 - 2) = 1$, so $V \otimes V \cong U \oplus U' \oplus V$. For the symmetric and exterior squares we need $\chi_V(g^2)$: the squares of $e$, $(12)$, $(123)$ are $e$, $e$, $(132)$, so $\chi_V(g^2) = (2, 2, -1)$. By Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)(vi), $$\begin{aligned}
\chi_{\Sym^2 V} &= \tfrac12(4 + 2,\; 0 + 2,\; 1 - 1) = (3, 1, 0), \\
\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V} &= \tfrac12(4 - 2,\; 0 - 2,\; 1 + 1) = (1, -1, 1).
\end{aligned}$$ The first is $\chi_U + \chi_V$ and the second is $\chi_{U'}$, so $\Sym^2 V \cong U \oplus V$ and $\bigwedge^2 V \cong U'$, as in Example [13.3.6](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#example-13-3-6).

**(3)** The group is abelian of order $4$, so each element is its own conjugacy class, and there are four irreducible representations, all $1$-dimensional (Proposition [13.1.7](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#proposition-13-1-7)); indeed $4 \cdot 1^2 = 4$. They are the elements of the dual group: for $(a, b) \in \{0, 1\}^2$, the character $\chi_{ab}(x, y) = (-1)^{ax + by}$.

<div class="table-wrap"><table class="tex-table has-stub"><thead><tr><th scope="col" class="c"></th><th scope="col" class="c">$(0,0)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(1,0)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(0,1)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(1,1)$</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{00}$</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{10}$</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">$-1$</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">$-1$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{01}$</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">$-1$</td><td class="c">$-1$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{11}$</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">$-1$</td><td class="c">$-1$</td><td class="c">1</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

**(4)** (a) A vector $\sum_s c_se_s$ is invariant if and only if $c_{gs} = c_s$ for all $g$ and $s$, that is, if and only if $s \mapsto c_s$ is constant on each orbit. So the sums $\sum_{s \in O}e_s$, one for each orbit $O$, form a basis of ${\CC}[S]^G$. By Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1) and Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)(v), the number of orbits is therefore $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}|S^g|$, which is Burnside’s lemma.

(b) The line spanned by $\sum_se_s$ is a copy of the trivial representation, $V_S$ is a subrepresentation complementary to it, and $\chi_{V_S}(g) = |S^g| - 1$. The action is transitive (given $s, s'$, choose $t \neq s$ and $t' \neq s'$, and use double transitivity), so by (a), $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g|S^g| = 1$. The diagonal $\{(s, s)\}$ and its complement are the orbits of $G$ on $S \times S$, and $|(S \times S)^g| = |S^g|^2$; so by (a) applied to $S \times S$, $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g|S^g|^2 = 2$. Since $\chi_{V_S}$ is real, $$H(\chi_{V_S}, \chi_{V_S}) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\bigl(|S^g| - 1\bigr)^2 = 2 - 2 \cdot 1 + 1 = 1,$$ and $V_S$ is irreducible by Corollary [13.5.7](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-7). The group $S_n$ acts doubly transitively on $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ for $n \geq 2$, and $V_S$ is then the standard representation.
:::
:::
